candidates.attacker_control: The raw password passed to matches() is fully attacker-controlled during authentication (login form, Basic auth, resource-owner password grant, etc.). The stored encoded password is not attacker-controlled, but the attacker chooses the candidate credential that is verified against it.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I explicitly checked the counter-argument that BCrypt truncation would make any 72-byte prefix of a long password match: BCrypt.streamtowords wraps with `% data.length`, so the entire password is consumed and two different non-periodic >72-byte passwords do NOT collide; a plain truncation bypass is therefore not demonstrated. I also verified BCryptPasswordEncoder's encoded-password format regex (line 129), null handling, and constant-time comparison via BCrypt.equalsNoEarlyReturn/MessageDigest.isEqual, and the DelegatingPasswordEncoder/{bcrypt} dispatch path. The finding rests on the absent 72-byte bound combined with the cyclic key schedule, not on a truncation bypass.
candidates.impact: Credential verification does not bind acceptance to the exact password that was set. Where a user's stored password is periodic (e.g. a repeated unit), a shorter base string that is not the user's password authenticates successfully, and where password policy allows >72-byte passwords, verified credentials/derived hashes are inconsistent with standard BCrypt semantics relied upon by other components and migrations. This is an authentication-acceptance weakness in a core credential verifier.
candidates.prerequisites: Application verifies credentials with BCryptPasswordEncoder (directly or via DelegatingPasswordEncoder with the 'bcrypt' id). The candidate password is attacker-supplied and either (a) is longer than 72 bytes, where Spring Security's cyclic use of the whole password diverges from every standard BCrypt implementation that truncates at 72 bytes, or (b) corresponds to the periodic key stream of the stored password (a stored password that is a repetition of a shorter unit, e.g. 'abcabc...' is matched by its shorter base unit 'abc').
candidates.root_cause: BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches(CharSequence, String) (crypto/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/crypto/bcrypt/BCryptPasswordEncoder.java:120-134) accepts unbounded raw password input and passes it directly to BCrypt.checkpw -> hashpw(byte[], String, true) -> crypt_raw -> ekskey/key. BCrypt.streamtowords (crypto/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/crypto/bcrypt/BCrypt.java:360-378, called from key/ekskey at lines 416-464 and hashpw at 588-604) consumes the key with `off = (off + 1) % data.length`, i.e. as an infinite repetition of the entire raw password. No length check or truncation to the algorithm's 72-byte width exists anywhere in the encoder or the BCrypt primitive.
candidates.title: BCryptPasswordEncoder does not enforce BCrypt's 72-byte password bound and verifies the full cyclic password stream
candidates.trace: matches(raw, encoded) -> BCrypt.checkpw(raw, encoded) (BCrypt.java:762-765) -> hashpwforcheck -> hashpw(byte[], salt, for_check=true) -> crypt_raw -> ekskey/key -> streamtowords, which repeatedly indexes the password bytes modulo data.length (BCrypt.java:372). Because the effective key material is the password repeated indefinitely, two different raw strings map to the same key stream whenever one is a whole-number repetition of the other (e.g. hash('abc') equals hash('abcabc')), and for raw inputs longer than 72 bytes the derivation is not the standard BCrypt derivation at all. matches() then compares the recomputed hash against the stored hash, so a raw input whose cyclic stream collides with the stored password's stream is accepted as a valid credential. There is no post-check that binds the verified bytes to the original password length.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and the exact CVE-to-file mapping was not confirmed from repository metadata (no CVE identifiers, changelog, or fix commit present in the snapshot). The practical exploitability depends on the application's password policy (whether >72-byte or periodic passwords are actually accepted/stored), which is deployment-specific. Whether the corresponding upstream fix rejects or truncates long passwords could not be inspected offline.
candidates.weakness_type: Authentication bypass / improper handling of password length in credential verification (CWE-287, CWE-1289)

coverage_summary: Scope per get_source_scope: 2023 model-visible files, 0 excluded symlinks/sensitive-name files, 0 files over 5 MiB, binary/NUL-containing files refused (none encountered in the Java sources reviewed). Test sources (src/test) and documentation/adoc sources are absent from the snapshot, so only main sources and build files could be reviewed. I read or searched: crypto password encoders (BCryptPasswordEncoder, BCrypt, DelegatingPasswordEncoder, SCrypt, Argon2, Pbkdf2), core authorization/method-security machinery (AuthorizationAdvisorProxyFactory, AuthorizeReturnObject*, AuthorizationMethodPointcuts, AuthorizationManagerBefore/AfterMethodInterceptor, interceptor order), config method-security wiring (PrePostMethodSecurityConfiguration, MethodSecuritySelector/AdvisorRegistrar, AuthorizationProxyConfiguration*), web access/intercept and matchers (AuthorizationFilter, RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager, AntPathRequestMatcher, StrictHttpFirewall, PathPatternParserServerWebExchangeMatcher), oauth2-jose/client/core validators (JwtTimestampValidator, JwtIssuerValidator, JwtValidators, X509CertificateThumbprintValidator, DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver, OidcIdTokenValidator), ldap escaping (LdapEncoder), and selected acl JDBC/permission classes. Broad literal searches covered ObjectInputStream, ProcessBuilder, createStatement, toLowerCase(), equalsIgnoreCase, gh- issue references, and 6.3.x @since markers.
limitations: No execution, tests, scanners, or CVE/OSV metadata were available; all conclusions are static source reasoning only.

The snapshot's version 6.3.8-SNAPSHOT was used to infer the fix window, but no changelog, git history, or CVE identifiers exist in the snapshot, so the mapping of this case to a specific CVE/fix is unconfirmed.

Large security-relevant areas were not exhaustively read: SAML2 OpenSaml4AuthenticationProvider/verification utils, WebFlux server filters, full oauth2-client grant flows, rsocket, messaging, cas, data and taglibs modules.
For the submitted candidate, the deployment precondition (applications accepting >72-byte or periodic passwords and using BCryptPasswordEncoder) was not verifiable from the repository.
The reported candidate is a lead derived from source evidence, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

rejected_leads.reason: Inspected AuthorizeReturnObject, AuthorizeReturnObjectMethodInterceptor, AuthorizationMethodPointcuts, AuthorizationAdvisorProxyFactory, AuthorizationProxyConfiguration, ReactiveAuthorizationProxyConfiguration and MethodSecurityAdvisorRegistrar. Class-level support appears present (@Target({TYPE,METHOD}), class-level AnnotationMatchingPointcut union, advisor registered via MethodSecurityAdvisorRegistrar). I could not construct a concrete source-level trace where the returned object is left unproxied while the annotation is present, so this remains a rejected/unconfirmed lead rather than a candidate.

A true return when both raw and encoded passwords are null is a genuine-looking authentication-acceptance hazard if a caller can pass two nulls, but the code path is long-standing upstream behavior and is not tied to the 6.3.8-SNAPSHOT change window; it is at most a hardening issue in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL injection / deserialization / command execution in ACL, config and core modules
rejected_leads.reason: Targeted searches for createStatement/Statement concatenation in acl, ObjectInputStream usage, ProcessBuilder, and other classic sinks found only the expected MethodSecurityMetadataSourceAdvisor readObject and JDBC parameterized statements; no unvalidated attacker-controlled sink was traced.

The AntPathRequestMatcher SubpathMatcher already lower-cases with Locale.ROOT (web/.../AntPathRequestMatcher.java:307,315) and no remaining toLowerCase()/equalsIgnoreCase path was found that would let request casing bypass an authorization rule.

JwtTimestampValidator, JwtIssuerValidator, JwtValidators, X509CertificateThumbprintValidator and OidcIdTokenValidator contain the expected required-claim and fail-closed checks; no concrete validation gap was identified.

summary: Reviewed the Spring Security 6.3.8-SNAPSHOT snapshot (2023 model-visible files; tests, docs, and samples stripped). I traced security-critical paths in crypto (password encoders, BCrypt), core method authorization (@PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize/@AuthorizeReturnObject plumbing), web access/intercept + URL matchers + firewall, oauth2 (jose validators, client resolver, ID-token validator), ldap escaping, and acl JDBC usage. The strongest source-supported candidate is the BCrypt password-verification path: BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches() imposes no 72-byte password bound, and BCrypt's key schedule consumes the raw password cyclically, giving non-standard verification semantics (repetition/prefix equivalence and divergence from standard BCrypt for inputs >72 bytes). Nothing else inspected showed a concrete, traceable authorization-bypass or injection flaw. The 6.3.8-SNAPSHOT version is consistent with a fix for CVE-2025-22228 in this file, but I could not confirm that mapping from repository metadata.
